title: TCP Slow Start, Congestion Avoidance, Fast Retransmit, and Fast Recovery Algorithms
summary: Writes down four tangled congestion control algorithms in TCP: slow start, congestion avoidance, fast retransmit, and fast recovery. Implementations already used them but they had never been documented as standards. It was replaced by RFC 2581.

plainLanguage.summary: Start by sending a little, then more and more until the road gets crowded, then slow down. TCP carefully feels out how fast the road lets it go.

questions: how does tcp congestion avoidance work
subtitle: The congestion control algorithms that let TCP feel out how fast the network can go.

tldr.problem: TCP implementations had four critical congestion control algorithms (slow start, congestion avoidance, fast retransmit, fast recovery) that worked in practice but had never been formally documented as standards, leading to inconsistency and undocumented behavior.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC documents how TCP starts by sending one segment, doubles the transmission rate for each acknowledgment received until congestion is detected (slow start), then grows the sending rate linearly (congestion avoidance). When packet loss is detected, fast retransmit resends the missing segment immediately instead of waiting for a timeout, and fast recovery continues congestion avoidance rather than dropping back to slow start.
tldr.outcome: This RFC standardized algorithms that were already widely deployed, making TCP behavior explicit and interoperable. It was replaced by RFC 2581, which added further refinements.

today: RFC 2001 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 2581. These four algorithms remain fundamental to TCP and are implemented in all modern TCP stacks. Further refinements have been standardized in subsequent RFCs, but the core principles outlined here—exponential probing in slow start, linear growth in congestion avoidance, and fast recovery of lost segments—remain the foundation of TCP congestion control.

sections.title: TCP Congestion Control Fundamentals
sections.content: This RFC documents four critical algorithms that TCP uses to manage the rate at which it sends data, avoiding network congestion. Implementations already used these algorithms, but they had never been formally written down as standards. The algorithms are intertwined: slow start finds the initial safe sending rate by exponentially increasing the window until congestion appears, congestion avoidance increases the sending rate linearly once slow start completes, fast retransmit detects a lost packet from duplicate acknowledgments and resends it immediately (rather than waiting for a timeout), and fast recovery continues congestion avoidance after fast retransmit instead of dropping back to slow start. These algorithms were developed by Van Jacobson and appeared in 4.3BSD Tahoe (fast retransmit) and 4.3BSD Reno (fast recovery). RFC 1122 required TCP to implement slow start and congestion avoidance, but this RFC is the first to formally document all four together.
sections.plainLanguage: These are four tricks TCP uses to avoid overwhelming the network. They work together to find the sweet spot: fast enough to use the network, slow enough not to break it.

sections.title: Slow Start: Finding the Initial Rate
sections.content: When a TCP connection opens, the sender must discover how fast the network can carry data. The naive approach—sending up to the receiver's advertised window size immediately—can overwhelm routers between the sender and receiver, causing packet loss. Slow start prevents this by introducing a second window, the congestion window (cwnd), which starts at one segment (the sender's MSS, typically 512 or 536 bytes). Each time the sender receives an acknowledgment from the receiver, it increments cwnd by one segment. The sender transmits min(cwnd, advertised window) bytes at a time. This exponential growth—send 1, then 2, then 4, then 8 segments—rapidly probes the network's capacity while staying conservative enough to avoid packet loss on slow WAN links. When a router's buffer fills and packets are lost, the sender detects this and switches to congestion avoidance.
sections.plainLanguage: Start with 1 segment. Each time you get an acknowledgment, send 2. Then 4. Then 8. Double the pace until packets start getting lost, then switch strategies.

sections.title: Congestion Avoidance: Growing Carefully
sections.content: Once slow start finds approximately the right sending rate, congestion avoidance takes over to avoid overshooting. The TCP sender maintains two variables: cwnd (congestion window) and ssthresh (slow start threshold). When congestion occurs—indicated by a timeout or reception of duplicate ACKs—the sender saves half the current window size (but at least 2 segments) to ssthresh. If the congestion was a timeout, cwnd is reset to 1 and slow start restarts. When congestion avoidance is active (cwnd > ssthresh), the congestion window grows linearly: cwnd increases by segsize²/cwnd octets per acknowledgment, meaning it increases by at most one segment per round-trip time, compared to slow start's exponential growth. This linear growth allows the sender to approach the network capacity smoothly. After a loss event, the sender continues with a lower rate (one-half the prior rate, stored in ssthresh), avoiding the abrupt drop to one segment that would waste capacity.
sections.plainLanguage: Once you know roughly how much the network can handle, grow the sending rate one segment per round-trip time. If packets are lost, drop to half the rate and grow carefully from there.

sections.title: Fast Retransmit and Fast Recovery
sections.content: Fast retransmit improves on the standard TCP timeout mechanism. When a segment is lost, the receiver sends a duplicate ACK (acknowledging the same sequence number again) each time it receives an out-of-order segment, signaling that a gap exists in the stream. TCP normally waits for a timeout (on the order of seconds) to retransmit a lost segment. However, if three duplicate ACKs arrive in a row, the sender infers with high confidence that a segment was lost (three duplicate ACKs indicate the receiver got three more segments after the lost one), and immediately retransmits the missing segment without waiting for the timeout. This dramatically reduces recovery time. Fast recovery then handles congestion avoidance after fast retransmit, rather than resetting to slow start. When the third duplicate ACK arrives, ssthresh is set to half the current cwnd, the lost segment is retransmitted, and cwnd is inflated to ssthresh plus 3 segments (accounting for the 3 segments that caused the duplicate ACKs and are still in flight). Each additional duplicate ACK increments cwnd by one segment. When a new ACK arrives (acknowledging the retransmitted data and everything in between), cwnd is set to ssthresh. This approach maintains flow and avoids the drastic slowdown of slow start.
sections.plainLanguage: If three duplicate ACKs arrive, a packet was probably lost. Send it again right away instead of waiting. Do not drop all the way back to slow start—just halve your rate and keep most of your speed.
